newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Diplomats fear Milosevic crackdown after holidays.
newsitem.headline: Diplomats fear Milosevic crackdown after holidays.

text.p: Serbian demonstrators have ignored a ban on street marches but some diplomats fear police will pounce once the end-year holiday period ends in a few days.
"There is a limit to how much (President Slobodan) Milosevic can take without becoming a laughing stock in Belgrade," a senior Western envoy said.

"His authority is crumbling as we speak, among the army, the police, his own Socialist party ranks and even the apolitical public. His credibility in the West is almost gone. He must put a stop to this one way or the other."
Hundreds of thousands of protesters paralysed downtown Belgrade on Monday night in an Orthodox Christmas Eve procession to St Sava Cathedral for midnight mass.
It was the biggest turnout in 50 straight days of protests against election fraud and the latest insult to Milosevic's autocratic government, irresolute and isolated as never before.
Diplomats believe he has not stamped out the demonstrations so far because of uncertain support even among the stoutest pillar of his authority -- the dreaded state security police.
"There is no way that he could have cracked down amid Christmas Day-New Year celebrations but a couple of days later is a different matter altogether," the diplomat said.

A quarter of a million revelling protesters clogged Belgrade on international New Year's Eve, December 31, and outwitted the anti-march edict on January 5 by jamming the Yugoslav capital with a cavalcade of cars.

The Orthodox New Year next week will be another occasion for an outpouring just as jolly as political, like every demonstration staged over the past two weeks. Security police have stayed out of sight.
But tensions are threatening to boil over with a reported bomb blast on Monday night outside the headquarters of the leftist party JUL, led by Milosevic's wife.
Diplomats tend to believe the bomb was staged by neo-communist zealots who want to force the authorities into prohibiting rallies in squares next week.
Zoran Djindjic, co-leader of the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition, quoted informants in the government as saying gatherings in squares would be banned on January 12.

Extending the ban on assembly to pedestrian zones would, if enforced, silence the daily displays of defiance that have badly dented the ramparts of one-party power in Serbian-led Yugoslavia dating to 1945.
Djindjic vowed the movement, carried by popular discontent over a ruined state-run economy, SPS corruption and oblivious state-dominated media, would find other ways of agitating.

But the bomb incident heightened fears among Zajedno supporters and Western diplomats of "provocateurs" infiltrating opposition ranks to stage attacks on symbols of state authority, handing Milosevic a pretext to smash the protests.

Zajedno is anxious not to lose its image as a movement for peaceful democratic change because that has won it support from parts of the power structure including army officers and the long-docile Orthodox church, as well as the West.

Investigators of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) confirmed Zajedno's claim to have triumphed in municipal elections in 15 of Serbia's 18 largest cities and including Belgrade.
Serbian authorities invalidated the outcome on the basis of unspecified "irregularities".

Until now, Milosevic has been known as the Balkans' master political survivor for weathering the breakup of federal Yugoslavia and war in Croatia and Bosnia, both started by his nationalist disciples, followed by economic collapse.

To prevail now, Milosevic must decide whether to honour the election result in full to rehabilitate his rule and lure financial aid from the West, or unleash his police to reassert SPS domination and risk ostracism by the world.

Even if driven off the streets, Zajedno supporters say they will start refusing to pay utility bills and bombarding the switchboards of ministries, SPS-run radio and television and other institutions to snarl government activity.
